newsitem.title: UK: UK gilts settle 10/32 lower on renewed rate woes.
newsitem.headline: UK gilts settle 10/32 lower on renewed rate woes.

text.p: UK gilt and short sterling futures ended Monday sharply lower as renewed fears over higher interest rates infected the markets.

The short sterling strip shifted down as the market started to discount a half point rate rise before the end of the third quarter, and gilts suffered a bout of profit taking after Friday's smart recovery.
"I think what we've seen today may be the major move before the budget. I can't see it going much lower than this," said a trader at a GEMM.
Nigel Richardson, head of bond research at Yamaichi International Europe, agreed.
"I think we're in for a period of sideways trading between now and the budget."
The September gilt future settled at 113-06, down 10/32.

Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown will deliver his first budget on July 2. Markets are keen to see the extent of any fiscal tightening to see if it is enough to take the pressure off interest rates.
Richardson said he expects a half point rate rise during the summer unless some very significant tax rises are made.
"And I don't think gilts are going to like that. They liked the first two quarter point rises (since May) but the next two may be a different matter."

He said the prospects for the yield spread to Bunds -- currently 156 basis points compared with 153 on Friday -- are not good short term. "I think we are in for a period of underperformance short term, although later this year the spread should narrow."
But despite current volatility, traders said the auction on Wednesday of 2.0 billion stg 10-year gilts should go well.
"It may be a largely domestic affair, but it should be well covered -- probably twice over," said the trader.
September short sterling settled at 92.96, down 0.08 on the day and almost fully discounting a half point rate rise by the end of September.
Losses were mirrored in the deferred contracts which lost between seven and 10 basis points as the interest rate outlook deteriorated.
"The real test is the budget. If we get only a small tightening (in fiscal policy) it's all down to the Bank of England to slow demand," said the trader.
